title: Representation-split Carleman lattice Boltzmann with near-unit step success probability on quantum computers
abstract: The Carleman lattice Boltzmann method replaces the quadratic collision of the lattice Boltzmann equation by a linear map on a lifted state. Existing block encodings of this map succeed with probability $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-2}$ per step, so that the probability of a multi-step evolution decays exponentially with the number of steps. This study develops multi-relaxation-time Carleman lattice Boltzmann, a representation split in which the Carleman-lifted collision is performed in a moment basis on the amplitude-encoded state, while streaming remains a permutation in population space. The level-2 hierarchy closes under collision but not under streaming, which generates the work of pressure, advection and stress on the momentum flux. The state therefore remains the full pair array, and the moment representation is an orthogonal change of basis of the population one, with identical dynamics and truncation error. The operator to be block encoded changes with the basis, and with it the success probability of a quantum step. In the weighted Hermite basis with the amplitude encoding $f_i/\sqrt{w_i}$, the relaxation is a diagonal operator of norm one, and the level-2 collision stage becomes this diagonal plus a sparse coupling from products of conserved moments. A structured block encoding of this form raises the single-step success probability on the D2Q9 lattice from $10^{-2}$ for the best population encoding to 0.98. With the pair sector in relative coordinates and scaled, one step requires $O(\log^2 N)$ Toffoli gates and is verified by statevector simulation. The encoding and readout overhead of a $T$-step run is then polynomial in $T$ and $N$ rather than accumulating a factor $p^T$. For resolved flows, the remaining exponential loss in coherent multi-step Carleman lattice Boltzmann evolution is set by the non-equilibrium norm relaxed by dissipation rather than by the block encoding.

title: A Rydberg atom array coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity
abstract: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about $3~\mathrm{mV/cm}$ rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within $7.5~\mu\mathrm{s}$, well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of $3\%$ and $5\%$, respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.

title: A differentiable PCA-GPR surrogate framework for full-transient Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification of black-box nuclear thermal-hydraulic systems
abstract: Complex transient energy systems require uncertainty-quantified predictions, but Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification (IUQ) is often impractical because posterior sampling with high-fidelity system codes requires many expensive full-transient simulations. This study develops a surrogate-assisted Bayesian IUQ framework that makes full-time-series calibration practical for the NACIE heavy-liquid-metal natural-circulation loop. The key innovation is to transform a black-box transient simulator into a differentiable probabilistic emulator by combining principal component analysis with Gaussian process regression (PCA--GPR). The surrogate reconstructs complete multichannel temperature and mass-flow histories from a compact latent representation, preserving dominant temporal and cross-channel correlations while enabling automatic differentiation of the log posterior. This allows both gradient-free ensemble slice sampling and gradient-informed sampling with the No-U-Turn Sampler and Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo. Five principal components capture more than 99\% of the output variance, and the surrogate achieves normalized root-mean-square errors below 2\%. Compared with direct Flownex SE evaluations, the surrogate reduces likelihood-evaluation cost by approximately 3000-fold while preserving posterior statistics and correlations. Posterior predictive analyses show reduced bias, narrower intervals, and improved agreement with measurements and independent validation.

title: Localized high-Q resonances enable electrically defined beam steering in lithium niobate metasurfaces
abstract: High-speed beam steering for LiDAR and optical communication requires independent, reconfigurable control of optical phase. We demonstrate a metasurface combining lithium niobate's Pockels effect with high-Q (Q > 1700) silicon guided-mode resonance nanoantennas whose localized resonances allow individual electro-optic control at a 1 $\mu$m pitch. Identical arrays steer light to 53.5$^\circ$ or 32.4$^\circ$, with the angle set by the bias pattern rather than antenna geometry. We measure 18.0% 0th-order modulation depth, 0.09% of incident power in the steered order, and a 940 MHz detected modulation bandwidth. Mode-overlap analysis shows how inter-element coupling limits usable Q, providing design rules for compact, high-speed beam steering.

title: Constrained Nuclear-Electronic Orbital Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory for Excited-State Dynamics with Nuclear Quantum Effects
abstract: Nuclear quantum effects can strongly influence excited-state processes involving light nuclei, yet their inclusion in practical molecular dynamics remains challenging. We develop constrained nuclear-electronic orbital time-dependent density functional theory (CNEO-TDDFT), which incorporates quantum-nuclear delocalization into full-dimensional effective excited-state potential energy surfaces while retaining the formal structure and computational scaling of conventional TDDFT. Analytic gradients are also developed, enabling efficient on-the-fly excited-state dynamics. CNEO-TDDFT substantially improves excited-state vibrational frequencies involving hydrogen motion and reduces the root-mean-square deviation from experiment from 113 cm$^{-1}$ to 26 cm$^{-1}$. For excited-state proton transfer in 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline (HBQ), CNEO-TDDFT yields a characteristic transfer time of 14.0 fs, compared with 25.5 fs from conventional TDDFT, consistent with the experimentally inferred ultrafast timescale of 12$\pm$6 fs. These results establish CNEO-TDDFT as an accurate and efficient framework for excited-state dynamics with nuclear quantum effects.

title: Machine Learning Surrogate Model for Accelerating InGaAs/GaAs Quantum Well Laser Design
abstract: A machine-learning surrogate model based on a multi-layer perceptron neural network is used to predict six laser performance metrics for an indium gallium arsenide quantum well laser given epitaxial layer parameters as inputs. The surrogate model was trained on simulation data from a set of 4999 designs which were generated by varying epitaxial layer parameters and simulating each design with Harold to extract performance metrics. The model predicts all 6 chosen metrics with a coefficient of determination, $R^2$, greater than 0.91 on a held-out test set and demonstrates a $\sim 10^6 \times$ speed up compared to full device simulations. The model is used to search across 1 million potential epitaxial designs in the parameter space and find designs that minimize threshold current and internal loss. Using the surrogate, rather than full device simulation, reduces computation time for a million designs from 231 days to $\sim$2 minutes on a standard laptop. It is also demonstrated that use of the Swish activation function, rather than ReLU, together with engineered input features - i.e. derived quantities calculated from the base model inputs - raise the mean $R^2$ from 0.88 to 0.94 without additional training data, and reduce the mean absolute percentage error from $1.78 \pm 0.08 \%$ to $1.17 \pm 0.09 \%$.

title: Acoustic Illusion of a Rigid Object for a Moving Emitter via Equivalent Surface Control
abstract: We report a three-dimensional acoustic illusion of a rigid object illuminated by an emitter moving along an arbitrary trajectory. The object is absent: control sources are arranged around its location, the closed surface they define being termed the equivalent surface. Driven by the field the object would have scattered onto this surface, the sources radiate, by the Kirchhoff--Helmholtz representation, that same field beyond it. The control signals follow in closed form from a time-dependent physical optics formulation that we derive for a moving emitter, in which the motion enters analytically through the acoustic travel times, so that the scattering problem need not be re-solved at each emitter position, nor the propagation domain discretized. For objects too large to enclose, the signals are mapped onto an internal surface, an option whose advantages and penalties are discussed. Numerical simulations validate the method in both configurations.

title: Watt-level single-cavity dual-comb laser at 2.1 $μ$m wavelength
abstract: Compact ultrafast laser combs around the 2 $\mu$m atmospheric transmission window are of growing interest for direct spectroscopy and as drivers for nonlinear conversion to otherwise hard-to-reach spectral regions. Dual-comb systems in this region remain very scarce: existing implementations rely mostly on nonlinear conversion, resulting in complex systems with poor conversion efficiency and overall low average and peak power. In this paper, we report on a watt-level dual-comb laser directly emitting at 2.1 $\mu$m. The system is based on a single-cavity, soft-aperture Kerr-lens mode-locked (KLM) laser using a broadband holmium (Ho)-doped CaAlGdO$_4$ (CALGO) gain crystal. The laser delivers a total output power exceeding 2 W (1 W per comb) with a sub-100-fs pulse duration (50 nm bandwidth) at a repetition rate of 96.5 MHz, corresponding to a pulse energy of 10 nJ and a peak power of 100 kW per comb. To assess the source's potential for future spectroscopic applications, we characterize the free-running dual comb in detail for frequency stability, phase noise, and relative intensity noise (RIN), and benchmark the achievable spectral resolution by measuring spectral modulations imposed by Fabry-Pérot etalons. Our system combines the compactness, high efficiency, and passive mutual coherence of a single-cavity oscillator with watt-level average power at 2.1 $\mu$m, making it a promising source for environmental sensing in the atmospheric transmission window, or as a driver for nonlinear frequency conversion, for example, to the MIR and THz regions.

title: Ambient-pressure effects on shock emission and liquid-shell expansion following optical breakdown inside water droplets
abstract: We experimentally investigate the deformation and breakup of micrometer-sized water droplets following nanosecond laser-induced breakdown in the finite-beam regime D0/Db~2 and over a range of ambient pressures. Simultaneous measurements of the liquid deformation and emitted shock wave enable the gas and liquid phase dynamics to be distinguished quantitatively. Under fixed external focusing conditions, the curved droplet interface focuses and internally reflects the incident light, leading to transient plasma formation within the liquid and generating the pressure load that drives droplet deformation. At low laser energies (El<1mJ), plasma formation localized near the rear droplet-air interface produces an interfacial bubble that expands into a thin liquid film susceptible to hydrodynamic instabilities and ultimately collapses under the action of surface tension. The internal pressure is partially released into the surrounding air, generating a propagating shock wave. At higher energies (El>1mJ), the droplet is ablated along the laser axis, resulting in the explosive formation of a liquid shell and multiple shock fronts, both exhibiting supersonic expansion velocities. While the shock wave dynamics are well described within the framework of strong blast wave theory, we show that the shell expansion can be understood as being driven by the pressure load generated during plasma expansion inside the droplet. Consequently, the droplet expands as a liquid shell that subsequently follows ballistic motion and ultimately undergoes complete atomization. Although changing surrounding gas density substantially alters the propagation of the emitted shock wave, the droplet morphology and expansion dynamics remain nearly unchanged, given the internal load of the plasma-driven pressure.

title: Ablation-Driven Selective Laser Direct Mass Transfer for Micro-LEDs with High Speed, Enhanced Gap Tolerance, and High Precision
abstract: Micro light-emitting diodes (micro-LEDs) offer superior performance for next-generation displays, yet their scalable manufacturing is severely bottlenecked by the mass transfer process from donor to receiver substrates. The existing laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT) methods are restricted by low throughput, limited selectivity, and long reaction times. In this study, we introduce a novel defocused direct laser ablation transfer (D-DLAT) method utilizing polyimide as a dynamic release layer. Whereas most indirect laser transfer methods trigger chip release followed by passive descent toward the receiver, D-DLAT directly ablates the release layer to actively propel the small-sized chips towards the receiver via ablation shock. By optimizing the ablation profiles and scanning paths, this method achieves high-speed transfer with significantly enhanced precision and robustness. We demonstrate the successful transfer of micro-LEDs ranging from 600 $\unicode{x03BC}$m down to 35 $\unicode{x03BC}$m in size, with a minimum reported placement error of less than 1 $\unicode{x03BC}$m, and a critical transfer gap of up to 50 $\unicode{x03BC}$m. Furthermore, the D-DLAT approach enables full selectivity, facilitating complex patterned transfers and array repitching operations that are essential for full-color display integration. Our findings indicate that D-DLAT effectively overcomes the fundamental limitations of current transfer technologies, demonstrating substantial potential for the scalable and high-yield manufacturing of advanced micro-LED displays. Ultimately, D-DLAT establishes a robust paradigm for the high-speed manipulation and heterogeneous integration of micro-optoelectronic devices, extending its profound implications beyond displays to the broader landscape of advanced micro-assembly and flexible electronics.

title: Optical Coherent Combining in Multi-Aperture Free-Space Receivers through Atmospheric Turbulence via Optically Computed Alignment Gradients
abstract: Multi-aperture reception converts spatial diversity into a coherent-combining gain, but only if the relative phase and polarization of the collected field replicas are aligned before they are summed. In a satellite-to-ground downlink the atmosphere perturbs amplitude, phase and polarization, so the alignment must track a fluctuating channel rather than a fixed offset. This paper proposes a new optical-domain combining scheme in which the alignment information is computed by light itself: the ascent directions that maximize the combined output power are formed by optical interference and read out directly as differential photocurrents of balanced detection, so no estimate of the channel, no deliberate perturbation, and no per-branch digital processing is needed to obtain them. Every branch is aligned against one shared reference - a passive tap of the combined field itself - so no independent laser or optical frequency lock is required, and the update directions of all branches are available simultaneously in a single averaging window without frequency, code, or time multiplexing. The data path needs a single dual-polarization coherent receiver regardless of the aperture count, and the readout is built from elementary parts only - a 3 dB directional coupler, static phase shifters, a Faraday rotator, and balanced photodiodes - so no 90-degree optical hybrid, mixer, or polarization-diverse hybrid is required. The phase and polarization loops are fixed-gain and division-free, and each branch carries one phase modulator and one polarization controller with no amplitude actuator. A closed-form combining-gain and loss budget is derived, the assumptions and limitations of the scheme are stated explicitly, and experimental validation remains open.

title: Vertical ionization energies from inverse generalized Kohn-Sham calculations at fixed electron density
abstract: The exact Kohn--Sham (KS) system must have its highest occupied orbital energy equal to the negative of the lowest vertical ionization energy (VIE). No comparable theorem connects the deeper occupied levels $\varepsilon_k$ to the higher VIEs $I_k$. Chong, Gritsenko and Baerends (CGB) established empirically that $I_k + \varepsilon_k\propto\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}}-\varepsilon_k}$. We ask whether a similar relation holds for the exact generalized Kohn-Sham (GKS) system, which incorporates a fraction $\alpha$ of Hartree-Fock exchange. We invert near-exact CCSD/aug-cc-pVQZ ground-state densities of LiH, LiF, H$_2$O, HF, CO, N$_2$ and F$_2$ at $\alpha = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0$ and obtain the exact GKS systems at each admixture. As the density is held fixed and only the operator is varied, the resulting occupied spectra separate the effect of exact-exchange admixture on orbital energies from its effect on the density, two contributions inseparable in a self-consistent hybrid calculation. The CGB relation holds broadly across the family, with a proportionality coefficient linear in $\alpha$, $c(\alpha)=c(0)-s\alpha$, where $c(0)=1.185\pm0.017$ eV$^{1/2}$ and $s=1.987\pm0.041$ eV$^{1/2}$, with $R^{2}\ge0.9996$ for H$_2$O, CO, HF and N$_2$. Using the response-potential matrix elements tabulated by Gritsenko, Braïda and Baerends, we decompose the CGB coefficient into response and spectroscopic parts, and find $s$ to agree with the homogeneous-electron-gas step-height coefficient $K_g = 1.9932$ eV$^{1/2}$, which we conjecture is its origin. The coefficient vanishes at $\alpha^{*}=0.597\pm0.008$. At $\alpha^{*}$ the HOMO-referenced GKS occupied levels satisfy $\varepsilon_k\approx-I_k$ across the whole occupied range. The zero crossing is fixed by the core orbitals; in the outer valence the CGB coefficient is already indistinguishable from zero at $\alpha=0$.

title: Interaction of Sustained Vortex Shedding with a Phononic Subsurface: Effect of Positioning and Resonant Characteristics
abstract: Phononic materials (PMs) have emerged as a promising candidate to passively and beneficially interact with unsteady flows. However, their fluid-structure interaction (FSI) with separated flows exhibiting sustained periodic vortex shedding remains completely unexplored. In this study, we use a high-fidelity immersed boundary method to investigate the strongly coupled, nonlinear FSI dynamics of vortex shedding from a fully separated flow over a flat plate, with an embedded PM subsurface (PSub) modeled as a grounded diatomic chain driving a compliant section on the flat plate. We probe the dependence of the coupled system dynamics on two parameters: (1) the PSub chordwise position, which sets its spatial relationship to the flow structure, and (2) the rate of growth of the resonant displacement amplitude of a PSub, a behavioral parameter identified as a key driving parameter in PSub interaction with latent vortex shedding in prior work. Simulation results show that these two parameters drive clear and systematic changes to the limit-cycle vortex shedding. The PSub chordwise position determines the limit cycle PM-FSI dynamics, which can be classified into four distinct regimes as a function of position, ranging from substantial amplification to strong attenuation of lift and drag oscillation amplitudes in the limit cycle. Results reveal a configuration that reduces lift oscillation amplitude by over 30% and drag oscillation amplitude by over 50% with less than 0.5% change in mean lift and drag. Displacement amplitude envelope primarily governs transient responsiveness toward the limit cycle, where its influence also depends on the chordwise position. We analyze characteristic frequencies, the phase relationship between PSub displacement and lift, and unsteady and mean flow fields of the vortex-shedding process to explain mechanisms by which the PM modifies the flow.

title: Rovibrational cross sections for the CO$_2$ $00^00$, $01^10$, $02^20$ and Fermi resonance states $10^00(1)$ and $10^00(2)$ in collisions with He atoms
abstract: We present quantum scattering calculations of CO$_2$-He state-to-state integral cross sections for 25 transition sets, covering pure rotational transitions within and rovibrational transitions between: the ground state $00^00$, the bend fundamental $01^10$, the bending overtone $02^20$, and the Fermi doublet states $10^00(1)$ and $10^00(2)$. Exact coupled-channel (CC) and coupled-states approximation (CSA) calculations are performed using a new five-dimensional potential energy surface. The calculations cover collision energies from 20 to 5220 cm$^{-1}$, sufficient to obtain converged rate coefficients over 100-800 K, and include initial rotational states for each transition up to at least $j=35$. We present an energy-grid algorithm for rovibrational quantum scattering calculations that minimizes the number of separate calculations required. The resulting cross sections exhibit a dominant $\Delta j=0$ propensity and parity-dependent patterns. For the benchmark $00^00,j' \leftarrow 01^10,j$ transition, thermally averaged rate coefficients reproduce available experimental data. A comparison between the CC and CSA cross sections shows that, for vibrational quenching transitions, the CSA cross sections increasingly deviate from the CC results with increasing initial rotational state $j$. Calculated integral cross sections cover collision energies and rotational states needed to derive rate coefficients for non local thermal equilibrium radiative transfer modeling of mid-infrared CO$_2$ spectra. The computationally simpler CO$_2$-He system allows the methodology and approximations to be tested at high collision energies and rotational states, helping assess their suitability for the more complex and astrochemically important CO$_2$-H$_2$ system.
authors: Floris F. S. van der Tak

title: Frequency comb stability, bistability, and self-starting in normal dispersion microresonators
abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that it is possible to generate frequency combs in normal dispersion microresonators by taking advantage of fabricated mode coupling that induces a mode split. In particular, photonic crystal resonators periodically modulate the microresonator's width, which geometrically creates mode coupling. In contrast to frequency combs generated by microresonators in the anomalous dispersion regime, which are typically generated using bright solitons, the frequency combs generated by normal dispersion regime microresonators are dark pulses that are commonly referred to as dark solitons or platicons. In this work, we examine the linear stability of platicons in the pump-detuning and pump-power parameter space as the mode split strength and cavity dispersion is varied. Our work reveals a broad region of stability for platicons. Our work also reveals the existence of fingers at high power at whose boundaries a sharp transition occurs and inside of which platicon solutions are bistable. Finally, we investigate the overlap of the region where platicons are stable with the region where continuous waves are modulationally unstable, and it is possible for a platicon to self-start. Simulations show that platicons consistently self-start inside this region.

title: A tutorial on quantum scattering theory and coupled-channel calculations of bimolecular collisions
abstract: Collisions between atoms and molecules govern how energy is exchanged and redistributed in the gas phase, underpinning phenomena from spectral line broadening and interstellar molecular excitation to the cooling and trapping of molecules. A quantitative account of these collisions requires connecting the theoretical description of the interaction between the collision partners to measurable quantities such as cross sections. However, scattering theory as presented in quantum mechanics textbooks does not readily translate into numerical methods. Here, we formulate the scattering problem in Dirac notation, as customary in present-day quantum mechanics courses, and show how to build a practical numerical framework from it. We derive the "coupled channel" representation of the scattering problem with correct asymptotic behaviour and introduce Numerov's method to obtain time-independent wavefunctions, from which we calculate cross sections, the observables measured in scattering experiments. Starting from single channel scattering, we build up to the realistic collision of a ground-state atom with a diatomic molecule.

title: Singular wave functions and quantum collapse in inverse-power potentials
abstract: Quantum collapse (QC) occurs under the action of the inverse-power potential U(r)=-U_{0}/(2r^{n}) in the framework of the Schroedinger equation. The corresponding stationary wave functions feature an infinite number of spatial oscillations at $r\rightarrow 0$. The ground state (GS) is missing in the presence of the QC, but the available bound states at finite energies may be physically relevant, as they are normalizable. This work aims to produce singular stationary wave functions. The analytical findings represent an asymptotic form of the stationary wave functions at $r\rightarrow 0$, which fill a continuous spectrum, and some exact solutions for the wave functions, obtained under appropriate conditions. As a regularized version, we also consider the potential truncated at a finite difference from the center. The regularized wave functions feature a finite number of spatial oscillations, the missing GS reappears, and the spectrum of the bound states is discrete.

title: Displacement-noise-free gravitational-wave detector using quantum tomography of photon orbital angular momentum states
abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) induce quantum transitions between photon orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) states with amplitudes $\alpha_{\pm}$. Exploiting this effect, we present a displacement-noise-free detection framework that extracts GW information from the OAM Hilbert space. Parametrized quantum state tomography of the GW-induced OAM sidebands enables a single V-shaped detector to resolve all seven wave parameters: the frequency, propagation direction, two polarization amplitudes, and initial phase of each polarization. Direct detection of the sidebands yields a weak signal of approximately $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{W}$. We therefore introduce a stronger reference state $r |0>_{\mathrm{P}}$, with $r=0.01$, to enhance the detected signal. For an arm length of $L=4\,\mathrm{m}$, $N=160$ round trips, a paraxial parameter of $\gamma=0.1$, an incident light power of $P_{\mathrm{BS}}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$, a wavelength of $\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=1064\,\mathrm{nm}$, and GW amplitudes of $A=10^{-18}$, we estimate sideband transition amplitudes of $|\alpha_{\pm}|\sim10^{-10}$ and signal powers of order $1\,\mathrm{nW}$, scaling as $P_{\mathrm{BS}}\alpha_{\pm}\propto P_{\mathrm{BS}}ANL\gamma/\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}$. The shot-noise-limited sensitivity floor is $S^{1/2}_n=1.6\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}^{-1/2}$. Because the scheme measures OAM transition amplitudes rather than differential arm lengths, it is intrinsically free from displacement noise and provides a broadband probe of GWs, specifically bridging the $0.1$--$10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ mid-frequency gap.

title: Large in-plane optical anisotropy in epitaxial CrN(113) films
abstract: CrN, a transition-metal nitride crystallizing in the cubic rocksalt structure, exhibits a unique combination of mechanical robustness, semiconducting behavior, and thermoelectric functionality. To date, however, CrN has been synthesized primarily as polycrystalline material or as epitaxial films grown along high-symmetry orientations such as (001) and (111). Here, we prepare epitaxial CrN(113) films on AlN(11\bar{2}2) templates by plasma-assisted molecular beam epitaxy. The low-symmetry interface and highly direction dependent lattice mismatch are expected to modify the physical properties of CrN relative to the bulk material. Indeed, variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry in the photon-energy range from 1.25 to 5 eV reveals a surprisingly strong polarization dependence of the optical response despite the nearly strain-free cubic crystal structure of the films. The pseudo-optical constants n and k differ by more than 10% for orthogonal in-plane polarizations throughout the investigated spectral range. We evaluate possible origins of this effect and conclude that it most likely arises from anisotropic surface morphology of CrN(113), which creates a metasurface acting as a subwavelength grating in the strongly absorbing regime.

title: Framework for atom-resolved decomposition of second-harmonic generation in nonlinear optical crystals
abstract: In this work, we develop a new framework for computing atom-resolved contributions to optical properties based on atoms-in-molecules (AIM) schemes. The formalism is independent of the specific AIM method and is made rigorous by partitioning momentum matrix elements into atomic contributions while exactly satisfying the relevant sum rules. Zincblende GaP provides a two-atom demonstration of the atom-resolved second-harmonic-generation (SHG) analysis using five AIM partitioning methods. The two-center Ga--P channels account for $80.6$--$82.2\%$ of the SHG response, despite the pronounced partition dependence of the atomic charges. We then apply the framework to six representative ultraviolet nonlinear-optical crystals: $\beta$-BaB$_2$O$_4$ (BBO), LiB$_3$O$_5$ (LBO), CsB$_3$O$_5$ (CBO), CsLiB$_6$O$_{10}$ (CLBO), KBe$_2$BO$_3$F$_2$ (KBBF), and LiCs$_2$PO$_4$ (LCPO). The atom-triplet decomposition shows that two-center channels dominate the principal SHG components, while on-site terms are smaller and multicenter terms provide an important secondary contribution. Although the AIM charges, detailed local percentages, and exact pathway ranks depend on the partition, the physical interpretation remains stable across the tested AIM methods. B/O-only pathways dominate the leading responses of KBBF and LBO. Mixed pathways involving B/O or P/O atoms and cations make substantial contributions to the leading responses of BBO, CBO, CLBO, and LCPO. The decomposition framework therefore establishes a quantitative connection between local response pathways and the bulk nonlinear-optical response.

title: Quantum analysis of a multi-frequency laser with a photonic time crystal
abstract: The present study considers the operation of a laser that incorporates a photonic time crystal (PTC), the purpose of which is to generate a field characterised by multiple widely separated optical frequencies. This laser is the subject of both a proposal and theoretical investigation. The laser comprises an active medium and a PTC within a small cavity constructed from two photonic crystals that are positioned in an overlapping configuration. PTC is modulated by an external field. The spikes in the laser field spectrum are separated by the PTC modulation frequency. The development of a quantum model of the laser with PTC has been achieved, and the analysis of a lasing mode with multi-frequency spikes has been made. The investigation focused on the study of lasing conditions, output power, and the lasing field spectra. The experimental realization of the multi-frequency laser with PTC under realistic conditions is discussed.

title: Optical chirality of membrane metasurfaces with broken in-plane symmetry
abstract: We study chiroptical properties of single-layer dielectric membrane metasurfaces with broken in-plane symmetry. Although chiral optics was long tied to structures lacking any mirror symmetry, planar (2D) chiral structures that retain a horizontal mirror plane now attract growing attention for their strong chiral optical effects. We explicitly show and explain how single-layer metasurfaces can achieve strong resonant chiral response. Although the single-layer geometry forbids conventional co-polarized circular dichroism, strong resonant conversion circular dichroism appears to be possible in particular wavelength ranges determined by the spectra of photonic eigenmodes. We explore its origin starting with a $C_4$ rotation-symmetric and in-plane mirror-symmetric membrane metasurface and applying to it various in-plane perturbations. Simultaneous breaking of the in-plane mirror symmetry and lifting the rotation symmetry unlocks resonantly enhanced circular conversion dichroism. We derive selection rules for this effect and trace its origin to eigenmode interference and intercoupling using chiral coupled-mode theory. Material absorption weakens the conversion dichroism produced by modes of opposite up-down parity, but it is essential for that produced by modes of the same parity.

title: Photon-conserving Raman soliton attractors in focusing and defocusing Kerr media
abstract: The sign of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient has long been regarded as irrelevant to the direction of the Raman-induced soliton self-frequency shift. Yet the standard generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) predicts a frequency shift that depends on the sign of the nonlinearity, which leads to an unphysical blue shift in the defocusing case. We resolve this inconsistency by deriving the time-domain form of the photon-conserving GNLSE (pcGNLSE) from its established frequency-domain counterpart. The derivation reveals that photon-number conservation imposes two sign modifications relative to the standard GNLSE: the Raman-shift coefficient acquires the absolute value of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient in place of its signed counterpart, and the self-steepening-Raman dissipation term likewise carries an absolute-value prefactor rather than a signed one. These two modifications jointly guarantee a universal spectral redshift and monotonically decreasing pulse energy during propagation, irrespective of the signs of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient and its frequency derivative. Applying the method of moments to the time-domain pcGNLSE with appropriate chirped ansätze, we derive closed-form evolution equations for five pulse parameters and establish explicit attractor conditions under which bright or dark Raman solitons propagate with constant peak power. Direct numerical integration of the pcGNLSE confirms all analytical predictions and demonstrates that the standard GNLSE fails qualitatively, predicting unphysical energy growth and spectral blueshift in the negative-nonlinearity regime. The results provide a rigorous analytical framework for Raman soliton dynamics in materials with negative third-order susceptibility, with direct implications for soliton-based devices in emerging semiconductor waveguide and microresonator platforms.

title: Gas release from metals under irradiation with elliptic Gaussian laser beam during LID-QMS analysis
abstract: Laser-induced-desorption quadrupole-mass-spectrometry (LID-QMS) diagnostics is considered as one of the candidate methods for the remote control of tritium inventory in the ITER first wall. Studies involving LID-QMS generally assume the circular shape of the laser spot on the analyzed surface. At the same time, the diagnostics laser source cannot be always positioned so as to irradiate tokamak tiles under normal angles, which results in the laser spot shape differing from the circular one. In this contribution, we analyze the tritium removal process under sample irradiation by an elliptic Gaussian laser beam, extending the results of our previous analysis [A.A. Stepanenko, Yu.M. Gasparyan, Physica Scripta 99 (8), 085604 (2025)]. The thermal desorption model governing the heat transport and tritium removal from the solid is formulated. The new analytical expression describing the sample temperature dynamics is derived. The developed model is used to examine the impact of the laser beam/spot ellipticity on the tritium desorption process from a tungsten sample. The conditions, under which the elliptic beam can be approximated with the circular one for the rapid assessment of the amount of desorbed tritium, are assessed.

title: $f$-2$f$ self-referencing for silicon nitride photonics via a heterogeneously integrated lithium niobate layer
abstract: Heterogeneous integration combines complementary material properties in a single photonic platform. Here, we demonstrate on-chip $f$-2$f$ self-referencing in a heterogeneously integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/LiNbO$_3$ platform, in which supercontinuum generation in a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide and second-harmonic generation in a LiNbO$_3$ layer are spatially separated and linked by adiabatic escalator couplers. Pumped by a 1560 nm mode-locked laser with 75 pJ on-chip pulse energy, we detect the carrier-envelope offset frequency with 30 dB signal-to-noise ratio in 300 kHz resolution bandwidth. A comparative measurement confirms that the second harmonic originates in the LiNbO$_3$ layer and indicates opportunity for further improvements through periodic poling. These results establish heterogeneous Si$_3$N$_4$/LiNbO$_3$ integration as a viable building block for self-referenced ultrafast pulse sources in low-loss Si$_3$N$_4$ photonics.

title: Integrated Open-Source Framework for Simulation of Transcatheter Pulmonary Valves in Native Right Ventricular Outflow Tracts
abstract: Pulmonary insufficiency is a consequence of transannular patch repair in Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF), leading to late morbidity and mortality. Transcatheter native outflow tract pulmonary valve replacement (TPVR) has become common, but assessment of patient candidacy and selection of the optimal device remains challenging. We demonstrate an integrated open-source workflow for simulation of TPVR in image-derived models to inform device selection. Machine learning-based segmentation of Computer Tomography (CT) scans was implemented to define the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT). A custom workflow for device positioning and pre-compression was implemented in SlicerHeart. Resulting geometries were exported to FEBio for simulation. Visualization of results and quantification were performed using custom metrics implemented in SlicerHeart and FEBio. RVOT model creation and device placement could be completed in under 1 minute. Virtual device placement using FE simulations visually mimicked actual device placement and allowed quantification of vessel strain, stress, and contact area. Regions of higher strain and stress were observed at the proximal and distal end locations of the TPVs where the devices impinge on the RVOT wall. No other consistent trends were observed across simulations. The observed variability in mechanical metrics across RVOTS, stents, and locations in the RVOT highlights that no single device performs optimally in all anatomies, thereby reinforcing the need for simulation-based patient-specific assessment. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a novel open-source workflow for the rapid simulation of TPVR, which, with further refinement, may inform assessment of patient candidacy and optimal device selection.

title: Empirical Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization from Encoded Unitary Designs
abstract: We introduce the Constraint-Enhanced Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (CE-QAOA), a shallow, constraint-aware ansatz that operates inside the one-hot product space [n]^m, where m is the number of blocks and each block is initialized in an n-qubit W_n state. We give an ancilla-free, depth-optimal encoder that prepares W_n using n-1 two-qubit rotations per block, and a two-local block-XY mixer that preserves the one-hot manifold and has a constant spectral gap on the one-excitation sector. At the level of expressivity, we establish per-block controllability, implying approximate universality per block. At the level of distributional behavior, we show that, after natural block and symbol permutation twirls, shallow CE-QAOA realizes an encoded unitary 1-design and supports approximate second-moment (2-design) behavior; combined with a Paley-Zygmund argument, this yields finite-shot anticoncentration guarantees. Algorithmically, we wrap constant-depth sampling with a deterministic feasibility checker to obtain a polynomial-time hybrid quantum-classical solver (PHQC) that returns the best observed feasible solution in O(S n^2) time, where S is a polynomial shot budget. We obtain two advantages. First, when CE-QAOA fixes r >= 1 locations different from the start city, we achieve a Theta(n^r) reduction in shot complexity even against a classical sampler that draws uniformly from the feasible set. Second, against a classical baseline restricted to raw bitstring sampling, we show an exp(Theta(n^2)) minimax separation. In noiseless circuit simulations of traveling salesman problem instances with n in {4,...,10} locations from the QOPTLib benchmark library, we recover the global optimum at depth p = 1 using polynomial shot budgets and coarse parameter grids defined by the problem size.

title: Time-Rescaled STIRAP Enables Compact Cascaded Frequency Conversion
abstract: In this letter we explore how full frequency conversion can be performed in shorter optical devices by using a STIRAP-like protocol modified by the time rescaling shortcut to adiabaticity. We first show a detailed, step-by-step process of how the coupled equations for two simultaneous three-wave mixing processes can be written in terms of a STIRAP-like system. From the properties of the STIRAP protocol, we know that the ensuing process will result in robust conversion, but require long propagation distances inside the bulk crystal or waveguide. We then apply the time rescaling shortcut to adiabaticty in the conversion process to create a TR-STIRAP protocol, showing that full and robust conversion is also obtained, but at a fraction of the propagation distance. We also show how the original shaping of the coupling coefficients required by the TR-STIRAP can be approximated by Gaussian functions with high conversion fidelity, thus simplifying the experimental implementation. Finally, a possible application of the new protocol is discussed in the context of single-photon detection in the MIR.

title: Simulating cavity QED with spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensates revisited
abstract: Simulating cavity quantum electrodynamics in synthetic platforms offers a route to studying light--matter physics without real photons. We reassess the frequently invoked analogy between harmonically trapped, spin--orbit-coupled atoms and the quantum Rabi and Dicke models, with particular emphasis on squeezing and entanglement. A single non-interacting atom realizes the quantum Rabi Hamiltonian exactly, up to elementary spin and phase-space rotations. For $N$ non-interacting atoms, however, the center-of-mass mode is only one member of a complete orthonormal set containing $N-1$ relative modes. We prove that, after all modes are included, the spin--spin terms generated by the collective mode cancel exactly against those generated by the relative modes. Equivalently, the original Hamiltonian is a sum of independent one-particle Hamiltonians and therefore cannot create interparticle entanglement from a separable state. Contact interactions invalidate this cancellation but do not remove the relative modes or turn the exact many-body Hamiltonian into a Dicke model. A one-mode Dicke description can arise only as a controlled low-energy approximation after all relevant relative excitations have been shown to be spectrally suppressed. We discuss this distinction together with experimental scales, finite temperature, and possible mode-selection strategies. We also distinguish the single-particle interference underlying density fringes from the interaction-stabilized stripe supersolid observed in many-body condensates.

title: Absorption and Phase-Contrast Microtomography Using Direct X-Ray Detection With Commercial Off-The-Shelf CMOS Sensors
abstract: This work presents high-resolution X-ray microtomography based on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) CMOS image sensors as direct detectors. The system uses a microfocus X-ray source in cone-beam geometry, enabling both absorption-contrast imaging, thanks to the sensor s intrinsic resolution, and phase-contrast imaging, by adjusting the object-to-sensor distance. A dynamic flat-field correction algorithm mitigates radiation-induced sensor degradation during long acquisitions. The setup provides voxel sizes from 3.9 microns to 5.2 microns, with an effective spatial resolution (FWHM) as fine as 9.6 microns in magnified phase-contrast mode (1.33x) and 21 microns in non-magnified absorption-contrast mode. Phase contrast enhances visualization of soft tissue boundaries that are difficult to visualize using absorption-contrast imaging in the same experimental configuration.
